effect_mechanism: Wide belts reduce storm-surge flooding behind the mangroves.
conditionality: Needs wide belts (thousands of metres) for surge; narrower belts help only to some degree.
justification: Spalding, M., McIvor, A., Tonneijck, F. H., Tol, S., and van Eijk, P. (2014). Mangroves for coastal defence. Guidelines for coastal managers & policy makers. Wetlands International and The Nature Conservancy. — p.8: "Wide mangrove belts, ideally thousands of meters across, can be effective in reducing the flooding impacts of storm surges occurring during major storms (also called cyclones, typhoons or hurricanes). This can significantly reduce flood extent in low lying areas."

effect_mechanism: Roots bind sediment, slow water and trap sediment, reducing shoreline erosion.
conditionality: Narrative statement with no size (graded slight by rule).
justification: Spalding, M., McIvor, A., Tonneijck, F. H., Tol, S., and van Eijk, P. (2014). Mangroves for coastal defence. Guidelines for coastal managers & policy makers. Wetlands International and The Nature Conservancy. — p.8: "The dense roots of mangroves help to bind and build soils. The above-ground roots slow down water flows, encourage deposition of sediments and reduce erosion."

effect_mechanism: Restored stands sequester carbon in biomass and soil compared with bare tidal flats.
conditionality: Compared with unvegetated tidal flats; restored stands remain below natural mangroves (lnRR -0.33). Graded on the lnRR band (0.64 > 0.35 = strong).
justification: Su et al. (2021). A meta-analysis of the ecological and economic outcomes of mangrove restoration. Nature Communications. — p.2: "Figure 2b suggests that when compared to unvegetated tidal ﬂats, restored mangroves have better restoration outcomes (RR′ = 0.43, 95% CIs = 0.23 to 0.63) and biogeochemical functions (RR′ = 0.46, 95% CIs = 0.24 to 0.68). Such patterns are also evident for individual functions such as carbon sequestration (RR′ = 0.64, 95% CIs = 0.35 to 0.94)"

effect_mechanism: Rewetting and revegetation start soil carbon accumulation at rates like natural sites.
conditionality: Inventory guidance (Tier 1 assumption), not a measured effect; says removals are potentially large.
justification: IPCC (2014). Chapter 4: Coastal Wetlands. In: 2013 Supplement to the 2006 IPCC Guidelines for National Greenhouse Gas Inventories: Wetlands. IPCC, Switzerland. — p.27: "Changes in soil carbon resulting from rewetting, revegetation and creation activities for mangroves, tidal marshes and seagrass meadows are estimated because they represent potentially large carbon removals from the atmosphere."

effect_mechanism: Restoring lost mangrove area adds above-ground carbon and avoids soil carbon loss.
conditionality: Modelled global totals, not per-hectare effects; graded by the narrative rule.
justification: Worthington, T., and Spalding, M. (2018). Mangrove Restoration Potential: A global map highlighting a critical opportunity. The Nature Conservancy, IUCN and University of Cambridge. — p.4: "Full restoration of the areas identified could enable: o Carbon sequestration in aboveground biomass amounting to 69 million tonnes of carbon, equivalent to annual emissions from 25,000,000 US homes; o The saving of 296 million tonnes of soil carbon stocks through a combination of avoided emissions and sequestration emissions, equivalent to annual emissions from 117,000,000 US homes; o The addition of commercial fisheries species in mangrove waters totalling 23 trillion young-of-year finfish and 40 trillion crabs, shrimp and molluscs; and o Protection from annual coastal flooding for hundreds of thousands of people."

effect_mechanism: Restored stands treat wastewater better than bare tidal flats.
conditionality: Compared with unvegetated tidal flats. Graded on the lnRR band (0.28 = moderate).
justification: Su et al. (2021). A meta-analysis of the ecological and economic outcomes of mangrove restoration. Nature Communications. — p.2: "Figure 2b suggests that when compared to unvegetated tidal ﬂats, restored mangroves have better restoration outcomes (RR′ = 0.43, 95% CIs = 0.23 to 0.63) and biogeochemical functions (RR′ = 0.46, 95% CIs = 0.24 to 0.68). Such patterns are also evident for individual functions such as carbon sequestration (RR′ = 0.64, 95% CIs = 0.35 to 0.94), nitrogen accumulation (RR′ = 0.45, 95% CI = 0.19–0.72), wastewater treatment (RR′ = 0.28, 95% CIs = 0.26 to 0.29)"

effect_mechanism: Restored mangroves hold more crab production and diversity than degraded or naturally regenerating stands.
conditionality: One taxon group (crabs); fish production and diversity showed no clear difference. Graded on the lnRR band (0.80 = strong).
justification: Su et al. (2021). A meta-analysis of the ecological and economic outcomes of mangrove restoration. Nature Communications. — p.4: "Conversely, restored mangroves exhibit higher levels of crab production and diversity compared to both naturally regenerated mangroves (RR′ = 0.79, 95% CIs = 0.38 to 1.20) and degraded mangroves (RR′ = 0.80, 95% CIs = 0.64 to 0.97)."

effect_mechanism: Fish production and diversity in restored mangroves vs bare tidal flats.
conditionality: A null: confidence interval spans zero (lnRR 0.33, CI -0.82 to 1.84). Measures fish production and diversity, not household food security.
justification: Su et al. (2021). A meta-analysis of the ecological and economic outcomes of mangrove restoration. Nature Communications. — p.4: "there is no major difference for phosphorus accumulation (RR′ = 0.06, 95% CIs = −0.08 to 0.21), crab production and diversity (RR′ = 1.03, 95% CIs = −0.64 to 2.70), and ﬁsh production and diversity (RR′ = 0.33, 95% CIs = −0.82 to 1.84)"

effect_mechanism: Restored mangrove area adds nursery habitat and young commercial fish and shellfish.
conditionality: Modelled global totals of juvenile fish and invertebrates; no link to catches or household food security stated. Graded by the narrative rule.
justification: Worthington, T., and Spalding, M. (2018). Mangrove Restoration Potential: A global map highlighting a critical opportunity.
